question: Using the Libyan patrol boat P662 ‘Murzuq’, the Libyan coastguard (LCG) interfered with SOS Humanity’s rescue of a boat in distress on 2 March 2024. The LCG threatened the crew of Humanity 1 with automatic rifles, fired into the water and forced the crew to abandon the rescue. The boat used was reportedly donated to Libya by the EU in 2023.

This incident is one among the many reported where the LCG has used EU equipment to forcibly intercept migrant vessels and return them to Libya, endangering the lives of those on board. Yet, there is no indication that the Commission has changed its relationship with the LCG, enabling and funding their systemic violations and violent pullbacks to a country where crimes against humanity are documented by the UN.1 1.
What does the Commission plan to do, as a member of the Frontex Management Board, to ensure that Frontex informs ships in the Mediterranean that they are not allowed to take people back to Libya?
What are the primary objectives of the EU’s cooperation with the LCG and are these being achieved?
How does the Commission evaluate its cooperation with the LCG and what indicators deem the work successful and worth continuing?
answer: 1. Frontex does not have competence under EU law to designate places for disembarkation. The Agency’s mandate in search and rescue (SAR) is limited to providing technical and operational assistance to Member States, as SAR is a national competence under EU and international law (2). 2.

When it comes to EU actions in support of the Libyan Coast Guard, the primary objective is to strengthen its capacity to carry out effective SAR operations, in full respect of international law and human rights. In this context, EU actions include the provision of equipment, training and expertise for the development of standard operating procedures, in close cooperation with Member States.

For example, so far over 200 officers have benefitted from training, always including a module on human rights and international maritime law, via the support to integrated border and migration management in Libya programme. 3.

It is essential to continue to engage with Libyan authorities, working closely with Member States and international partners, including United Nations agencies, to ensure SAR operations, in full respect of international standards and human rights.

In this context, the Commission is working closely with partners implementing EU programmes on additional and better exchange of information in SAR operations, increasing border management capacity, timely access of humanitarian actors at disembarkation points and SAR.

For instance, enhancing trainings on international maritime law and on operating procedures for SAR is a key tool to advance dialogue and information sharing, while at the same time improve standards.
